sections.title: Executive Summary
sections.guidance: A reader should understand the business in under two minutes.

questions.title: What is the business?
questions.example: A healthy fast-casual food business in Bacolod that provides convenient meals with standardized calories and macronutrients.

questions.title: Who is the primary customer?
questions.example: Working professionals aged 25–40 in Bacolod with enough disposable income to pay above mass-market meal prices for convenience, taste, and nutrition transparency.

questions.title: What problem are we solving?
questions.example: Healthy eating is difficult to sustain because planning, cooking, portion control, and repeated decisions consume time and effort.

questions.title: What is our solution?
questions.example: A focused menu with consistent portions and clearly communicated nutrition, available via dine-in, takeaway, and delivery.

questions.title: How does the business make money?
questions.prompt: How does the business make money?
questions.example: Primarily individual meal sales, with secondary revenue such as beverages, add-ons, or corporate orders only if they prove profitable.

questions.title: Why can this work?
questions.example: Existing alternatives prove demand for convenient food, while the proposed differentiation may support repeat behavior and acceptable margins.

questions.title: Key numbers
questions.example: Startup Cost: PHP ___ | Break-even: ___ orders/month | Expected Revenue: PHP ___/month | Expected Operating Profit: PHP ___/month | Payback: ___ months

sections.title: Vision & Purpose
sections.guidance: Define what the business is trying to become—and what it is not trying to become.

questions.title: Why should this business exist?
questions.example: Make the healthier everyday choice easier without asking customers to become nutrition experts.

questions.title: 3-year state
questions.example: A consistently profitable Bacolod business with reliable operations, repeat customers, and a management structure that does not require all founders in daily operations.

questions.title: 5-year state
questions.example: A proven model that can either expand or remain a strong cash-generating local business depending on which path creates the best outcome.

questions.title: What are we explicitly NOT trying to become?
questions.prompt: What are we explicitly NOT trying to become?
questions.example: We are not trying to maximize store count at any cost, compete as the cheapest provider, or create a business that permanently depends on founder labor.

sections.title: Customer
sections.guidance: Describe the actual buyer and the behavior that produces revenue.

questions.title: Primary customer
questions.example: Define age, income, location, occupation, lifestyle, purchase frequency, and decision criteria.

questions.title: Secondary customer
questions.example: Only include if the economics and acquisition path are meaningfully different.

questions.title: Customer behavior
questions.example: Where do they buy today? How often? What alternatives do they use?

questions.title: Buying trigger
questions.example: They need the solution now, discover us through a relevant channel, trust the offer, and accept the price.

questions.title: Reasons not to buy
questions.example: Price, habit, distance, trust, timing, preference, or another substitute.

sections.title: Problem
sections.guidance: Explain the problem in observable terms, not only as an opinion.

questions.title: Primary problem
questions.example: What repeated job, pain, cost, inconvenience, or unmet need are we solving?

questions.title: Frequency
questions.example: How often does the problem occur?

questions.title: Severity
questions.example: How painful or costly is it?

questions.title: Current alternatives
questions.example: How is the customer solving this today?

questions.title: Why are alternatives insufficient?
questions.example: Explain the gap without assuming customers are unhappy just because you would build something different.

sections.title: Product / Service
sections.guidance: Define exactly what is sold at launch and deliberately limit the initial scope.

questions.title: Initial offer at launch
questions.example: What can customers actually buy on Day 1?

questions.title: What will NOT be included at launch?
questions.prompt: What will NOT be included at launch?
questions.example: Reduce complexity and avoid treating future ideas as launch requirements.

questions.title: Core customer experience
questions.example: Describe discovery → purchase → delivery/use → repeat purchase.

questions.title: Quality standard
questions.example: Define what must always remain consistent: quality, timing, safety, service, accuracy, etc.

questions.title: Future products / services
questions.example: Only list credible extensions after the initial model works.

sections.title: Market & Competition
sections.guidance: Summarize the evidence from Business Idea & Validation rather than repeating all research.

questions.title: Market type
questions.example: Red / Blue / Mixed

questions.title: Why?
questions.example: Explain the sources of competition and the specific underserved angle, if any.

questions.title: Reachable market
questions.example: Use a practical launch market, not an inflated total population.

questions.title: Required market share
questions.example: Translate break-even into active customers, purchase frequency, or contracts.

questions.title: Key competitors / substitutes
questions.example: Summarize 3–5 businesses or behaviors customers already use.

questions.title: Why do successful competitors survive?
questions.example: Strong location, repeat demand, cost control, brand, distribution, or another economic engine.

questions.title: What must we do differently or better?
questions.prompt: What must we do differently or better?
questions.example: Choose the dimensions where we intend to win.

questions.title: If Blue/Mixed, why has nobody captured it?
questions.prompt: If Blue/Mixed, why has nobody captured it?
questions.example: Distinguish opportunity from lack of demand.

sections.title: Positioning & Value Proposition
sections.guidance: Make the reason to choose you specific and believable.

questions.title: Positioning statement
questions.example: For ___, who ___, our business is ___ that ___. Unlike ___, we ___.

questions.title: Why should customers believe us?
questions.example: Proof, process, expertise, transparency, consistency, or another reason for trust.

questions.title: What are we willing to compete on?
questions.prompt: What are we willing to compete on?
questions.example: Examples: reliability, quality, convenience, transparency, service.

questions.title: What are we NOT willing to compete on?
questions.prompt: What are we NOT willing to compete on?
questions.example: Example: being the absolute cheapest option.

sections.title: Business Model
sections.guidance: Explain how activity becomes revenue and profit.

questions.title: Primary revenue stream
questions.example: What creates most of the revenue?

questions.title: Secondary revenue streams
questions.example: Only include realistic, operationally compatible streams.

questions.title: Average selling price
questions.example: PHP ___

questions.title: Variable cost per sale
questions.example: PHP ___

questions.title: Contribution profit per sale
questions.example: PHP ___

questions.title: Monthly fixed cost
questions.example: PHP ___

questions.title: Break-even volume
questions.example: ___ / month and ___ / day

questions.title: Expected scenario
questions.example: Revenue / operating profit / margin

questions.title: Capacity-limit scenario
questions.example: Maximum realistic revenue / profit with the initial setup

questions.title: Why is the startup cost justified?
questions.prompt: Why is the startup cost justified?
questions.example: The investment is acceptable only if expected returns remain attractive after replacing assumptions with real quotes.

sections.title: Sales & Marketing
sections.guidance: Explain how customers are acquired and why the selected channels fit their behavior.

questions.title: How will the first 100 customers discover us?
questions.prompt: How will the first 100 customers discover us?
questions.example: Describe specific launch paths.

questions.title: Launch channels
questions.example: Facebook, TikTok, Google Maps, delivery platforms, partnerships, direct outreach, events—only where relevant.

questions.title: Why should each channel work?
questions.example: Connect the channel to observed customer behavior.

questions.title: Retention strategy
questions.example: What creates repeat behavior?

questions.title: Referral strategy
questions.example: If relevant, explain why customers would recommend the business.

questions.title: Marketing budget
questions.example: PHP ___ / month

questions.title: Key acquisition metric
questions.example: Cost per first purchase, repeat rate, orders per active customer, etc.

sections.title: Why Us
sections.guidance: Be explicit about founder advantages and gaps.

questions.title: Founder advantages
questions.example: Skills, local knowledge, relationships, technology, operations, capital, trust, industry expertise.

questions.title: Missing capabilities
questions.example: What critical knowledge or operating ability is absent?

questions.title: How will we fill the gaps?
questions.prompt: How will we fill the gaps?
questions.example: Hire, partner, outsource, learn, or use advisors.

sections.title: Founder Roles
sections.guidance: Make ownership of work and authority explicit.

questions.title: Founders
questions.example: Define what this person owns and what they can decide independently.

questions.title: Shared responsibilities
questions.example: Keep this list small; shared ownership often means unclear ownership.

sections.title: Decision Making & Governance
sections.guidance: Decide how the three founders make decisions before pressure creates conflict.

questions.title: What can one founder decide alone?
questions.prompt: What can one founder decide alone?
questions.example: Decisions inside their defined area and budget.

questions.title: What requires majority agreement?
questions.example: Material but reversible decisions.

questions.title: What requires unanimous agreement?
questions.example: Debt, major capital expenditure, ownership changes, founder compensation, sale, shutdown, or adding a co-founder.

questions.title: What happens when we disagree?
questions.example: Define discussion, evidence, escalation, and tie-breaking rules.

questions.title: How are important decisions recorded?
questions.example: Use a shared decision log with date, owner, decision, reasoning, and follow-up.

sections.title: Ownership & Money Between Founders
sections.guidance: Agree on ownership, capital, compensation, and what happens when contributions differ.

questions.title: Ownership and capital
questions.example:
Founder 1 ___% | Founder 2 ___% | Founder 3 ___%
Founder 1 PHP ___ | Founder 2 PHP ___ | Founder 3 PHP ___

questions.title: Founder compensation at launch
questions.example: Salary / no salary / reimbursement rules.

questions.title: When can founder salaries increase?
questions.example: Tie changes to business conditions, not arbitrary dates.

questions.title: What if more capital is required?
questions.prompt: What if more capital is required?
questions.example: Define whether it is debt, additional equity, or optional contribution.

questions.title: What if one founder cannot contribute?
questions.prompt: What if one founder cannot contribute?
questions.example: Define dilution, loan treatment, or other agreed handling.

questions.title: What if a founder wants to leave?
questions.prompt: What if a founder wants to leave?
questions.example: Define with legal advice: notice, vesting, buyback, valuation, and transfer restrictions.

sections.title: Legal & Company Setup
sections.guidance: Translate legal and regulatory requirements into a launch checklist.

questions.title: Company structure
questions.example: Selected structure or TBD.

questions.title: Registrations
questions.example: List required registrations.

questions.title: Permits / licenses
questions.example: List business- and industry-specific permits.

questions.title: Tax / accounting setup
questions.example: Who handles books, filings, payroll, and controls?

questions.title: Employment requirements
questions.example: Contracts, statutory benefits, payroll obligations, workplace rules.

questions.title: Industry-specific compliance
questions.example: Food safety, professional licenses, data rules, product standards, etc.

questions.title: Professional advice required
questions.example: Lawyer / accountant / permits specialist / industry expert.

sections.title: Location / Facilities / Equipment
sections.guidance: Define what the initial physical setup must accomplish and what it must cost.

questions.title: Location requirements
questions.example: Customer access, delivery radius, size, utilities, parking, visibility, etc.

questions.title: Maximum acceptable rent
questions.example: PHP ___ / month, with a reason linked to unit economics.

questions.title: Required equipment
questions.example: List only items needed for launch.

questions.title: Capacity of initial setup
questions.example: ___ sales / orders / customers per day.

questions.title: Primary capacity constraint
questions.example: Kitchen, staff, seating, machine throughput, delivery, or another bottleneck.

questions.title: Before signing a lease / contract
questions.example: Define non-negotiable go/no-go conditions.

sections.title: Suppliers & Inventory
sections.guidance: Reduce the chance that one supplier, material, or inventory decision can stop the business.

questions.title: Critical suppliers
questions.example: List the suppliers or inputs the business cannot operate without.

questions.title: Alternative suppliers
questions.example: Identify backup options.

questions.title: Supplier selection criteria
questions.example: Price, quality, reliability, terms, distance, consistency.

questions.title: Inventory policy
questions.example: Stock level, reorder point, shelf life, wastage target.

questions.title: Single points of failure
questions.example: Inputs, people, equipment, or contracts that could stop operations.

sections.title: Operations
sections.guidance: Design the repeated operating system, not just the opening day.

questions.title: Opening / operating hours
questions.example: Define schedule and why it matches demand.

questions.title: Daily operating flow
questions.example: Opening, preparation, service, quality control, closing.

questions.title: Weekly operating flow
questions.example: Purchasing, scheduling, inventory review, maintenance, marketing, finance.

questions.title: Quality controls
questions.example: How is consistency checked and recorded?

questions.title: Cash controls
questions.example: Who receives money, reconciles sales, approves expenses, and reviews discrepancies?

questions.title: Customer complaint process
questions.example: How are issues received, resolved, recorded, and learned from?

questions.title: What must be documented before launch?
questions.prompt: What must be documented before launch?
questions.example: SOPs, checklists, vendor list, recipes/specs, pricing rules, safety procedures.

sections.title: People & Hiring
sections.guidance: Connect staffing to actual operating capacity and service quality.

questions.title: Roles required at launch
questions.example: List positions, not names.

questions.title: Number of people required
questions.example: Headcount and shift assumptions.

questions.title: Expected monthly payroll
questions.example: PHP ___

questions.title: Hiring criteria
questions.example: Skills, reliability, attitude, licenses, experience.

questions.title: Training required
questions.example: What must be taught before independent work?

questions.title: Day-to-day manager
questions.example: Who runs the operation each day?

questions.title: Trigger for the next hire
questions.example: Define an operational trigger such as sustained capacity utilization or service delay.

sections.title: Technology & Systems
sections.guidance: Use technology where it improves control, visibility, or customer experience—not because it is interesting.

questions.title: Systems required at launch
questions.example: POS, accounting, inventory, scheduling, website, CRM, analytics, etc.

questions.title: What can remain manual initially?
questions.example: Avoid premature automation.

questions.title: What should be automated early?
questions.example: High-risk repetitive processes, financial controls, or customer-critical workflows.

questions.title: Who owns setup and maintenance?
questions.example: Assign one accountable owner.

sections.title: Financial Plan
sections.guidance: Turn the validation model into operating financial guardrails.

questions.title: Startup cost
questions.example: PHP ___

questions.title: Opening cash reserve
questions.example: PHP ___

questions.title: Monthly fixed cost
questions.example: PHP ___

questions.title: Unit economics
questions.example: Price / variable cost / contribution profit / contribution margin

questions.title: Break-even
questions.example: Monthly and daily volume

questions.title: Conservative scenario
questions.example: Revenue / loss or profit / cash impact

questions.title: Expected scenario
questions.example: Revenue / operating profit / margin

questions.title: Strong scenario
questions.example: Revenue / operating profit / margin

questions.title: Capacity-limit scenario
questions.example: Revenue / operating profit / margin

questions.title: Runway if sales are below plan
questions.prompt: Runway if sales are below plan
questions.example: ___ months

questions.title: Trigger for additional funding
questions.example: Define the condition and maximum acceptable amount.

sections.title: Key Assumptions
sections.guidance: List the assumptions that must be true for the plan to work.

sections.title: Key Risks
sections.guidance: Focus on risks that can materially damage economics, launch, trust, or continuity.

sections.title: Go / No-Go Conditions
sections.guidance: Define decision thresholds before sunk cost and emotion make the decision harder.

questions.title: We proceed to launch if
questions.example: Expected economics remain attractive after real supplier/rent/payroll quotes; required permits are feasible; founders can fund initial capital plus buffer.

questions.title: We delay if
questions.example: Critical information is still missing but can realistically be resolved without irreversible spending.

questions.title: We stop / abandon if
questions.example: Realistic pricing produces structurally negative unit economics, startup capital rises far beyond expected return, or a critical legal/operational constraint cannot be solved.

sections.title: Review Cadence
sections.guidance: Define what the founders inspect regularly so problems become visible early.

questions.title: Daily
questions.example: Cash/sales exceptions, customer complaints, safety/quality exceptions, critical operating issues.

questions.title: Weekly
questions.example: Sales, margin, volume, inventory, staffing, marketing results, major actions.

questions.title: Monthly
questions.example: P&L, cash position, assumptions, pricing, hiring, capital decisions, strategy changes.

sections.title: Pitch-ready Summary
sections.guidance: Use the completed plan to create a concise narrative.

questions.title: One-minute explanation
questions.example: Problem → Customer → Solution → Why now → Business model → Why us → Next step.

questions.title: Five-minute explanation
questions.example: Problem → Customer → Solution → Market → Competition → Business model → Economics → Why us → Execution plan → Risks → Ask / next step.
